title: What Einstein Really Thought About Zionism
the_thought: He thought Zionism should build a home, not a nation like the others.
hook: Israel asked Einstein to be president. He said no. People heard a man walking away from the Jewish state. He thought Zionism should build a home, not a nation like the others. For thirty years he had helped build that home. So why refuse the chair?

levels.name: The Chair
beats: November, 1952. Israel's first president is buried. An evening paper in Tel Aviv floats a successor. The greatest Jew alive. The prime minister tells his ambassador in Washington to ask. The man in Princeton is seventy-three. He likes equations. He does not like official functions. They send a letter anyway. Would he take the presidency if the parliament voted it. He would have to move. Take citizenship. Become a head of state. He writes that he is deeply moved, and ashamed that he cannot accept. He has spent his life with objects, he says. He has neither the ability nor the experience to deal with human beings and carry out official functions. The new country wanted a symbol the world already loved. He would not sit in the chair.

levels.name: The Ship
beats: Thirty-one years earlier, he did get on a ship. 1921. A chemist who ran the Zionist organization takes him across the Atlantic. Banquets. Tickets. Speeches in halls that smell of roast chicken. The prize they are selling is not a flag. It is a university that does not exist yet, on a hill in Jerusalem. Einstein is not a statesman. He has just watched a world war eat a generation, and he blames nationalism for the appetite. And still he goes. Because he has decided the Jews are not a church with optional membership. They are a people who keep being told they do not belong. A university is a home you can build without drawing a border. The university opens in 1925. He will later leave it his papers. That is Zionism as he first practiced it. Bricks. Books. Not a throne.

levels.name: The Measles
beats: Then he says the sentence people still weaponize. 1929. An interviewer asks if he is German or Jewish. He says he looks upon himself as a man. Nationalism is an infantile disease. It is the measles of mankind. So why help a national movement. In 1938, in a New York hotel, he tries to hold both thoughts in one speech. Judaism owes Zionism a debt, he says. It revived a sense of community. It saved people from need. And in the same hour he resists a Jewish state with borders, an army, and a measure of temporal power, no matter how modest. He would rather see a reasonable agreement with the Arabs, living together, than copy the nations that made Jews homeless. If necessity forces a state anyway, bear it with tact. That is not a parade. It is a worried yes.

levels.name: The Paper
beats: Necessity arrived. In 1948 there is a state. Einstein does not pretend it can be un-invented. He also does not clap for every party that claims it. That December he signs a letter in a New York newspaper. He and other Jews warn Americans not to treat a visiting party leader as the face of the new country. They say that party's methods look like the ones they had fled. No halo. No victory parade. A people with a home, they thought, still had to choose what kind of home. He could belong to the Jewish people and still refuse a certain kind of Jewish power. That split is the whole story. It is not a late conversion, and it is not a betrayal.

levels.name: The Answer
beats: So what did he really think about Zionism. He thought Zionism should build a home, not a nation like the others. A university on a hill. A refuge. A sense of community that kept people from disappearing. Not a throne, and not a holy army. When they offered him the highest chair in that new country, he kept his no. He would be a Jew. He would not be a head of state. If you needed him to bless every border, he would fail you. If you needed him to say Jews should have nowhere, he would fail you too.
A home is one argument. What he thought a bomb was for is another. That story is next.
